blocks.html: One of the most exciting aspects of Sonic Pi is that it enables you to write and modify code live to make music, just like you might perform live with a guitar.

This means that given some practice you can take Sonic Pi on stage and gig with it - kind of like a ‘coding DJ’ - but with the incredibly expressive power of code. So you can work at any level - from mixing pre-made ‘tracks’ like a regular DJ to writing everything from scratch. There’s no right or wrong - simply find what works for you.

Before we get into the real details of how Sonic Pi works in the rest of this tutorial, I’d like to give you an experience of what it’s like to live code. Don’t worry if you don’t understand much (or any) of this. Just try to hold onto your seats and enjoy…
Let’s get started, here’s a Quickstart card containing the code for a very simple live loop - the main building block for performing with Sonic Pi.

blocks.source:
live_loop :flibble do
  sample :bd_haus, rate: 1
  sleep 0.5
end

blocks.html: Now, press the Run button and you’ll hear a nice fast bass drum beating away. If at any time you wish to stop the sound just hit the Stop button. Although don’t hit it just yet… Instead, follow these steps:

items:
Make sure the bass drum sound is still running, then click the Edit
icon (the little pencil) to enter edit mode.
Change the sleep value from 0.5 to something higher like 1.
Notice how the drum speed has changed.
Finally, remember this moment, this is the first time you’ve live coded with Sonic Pi and it’s unlikely to be your last…

blocks.html: Remember you’re free to experiment and try things out. At some point you might get a bit lost and break the code. Don’t worry, that’s normal and once you’ve read this tutorial you’ll know how to fix it. For now simply hit the Reset icon (the circular arrow) and try again.
Ok, that was simple enough. Let’s add something else into the mix. Take a look at this card - it adds the line sample :ambi_choir, rate: 0.3 above sample :bd_haus:

blocks.source:
live_loop :flibble do
  sample :ambi_choir, rate: 0.3
  sample :bd_haus, rate: 1
  sleep 1
end

blocks.html: Now, play around. Change the rates - what happens when you use high values, or small values or negative values? See what happens when you change the rate: value for the :ambi_choir sample just slightly (say to 0.29). What happens if you choose a really small sleep value? See if you can make it go so fast your computer will stop with an error because it can’t keep up (if that happens, just choose a bigger sleep time and hit Run again).

blocks.text: Add and remove sounds with comments

blocks.html: Try commenting one of the sample lines out by adding a # to the beginning:

blocks.source:
live_loop :flibble do
  sample :ambi_choir, rate: 0.3
#  sample :bd_haus, rate: 1
  sleep 1
end

blocks.html: Notice how it tells the computer to ignore it, so we don’t hear it. This is called a comment. In Sonic Pi we can use comments to remove and add things into the mix.

Finally, let me leave you something fun to play with. Now, don’t try to understand it too much other than see that there are two loops - so two things going round at the same time. Now, do what you do best - experiment and play around. Here are some suggestions:

items: Try changing the blue rate: values to hear the sample sound change.
Try changing the sleep times and hear that both loops can spin round at different rates.
Try uncommenting the sample line (remove the #) and enjoy the sound of the guitar played backwards.
Try changing any of the blue mix: values to numbers between 0 (not in the mix) and 1 (fully in the mix).

blocks.html: Remember to press Run and you’ll hear the change next time the loop goes round. If you end up in a pickle, don’t worry - hit Stop, then hit the Reset icon at the top of the card and you’re ready to jam again. Making mistakes is how you’ll learn the quickest…

blocks.source:
live_loop :guit do
  with_fx :echo, mix: 0.3, phase: 0.25 do
    sample :guit_em9, rate: 0.5
  end
#  sample :guit_em9, rate: -0.5
  sleep 8
end

live_loop :boom do
  with_fx :reverb, room: 1 do
    sample :bd_boom, amp: 10, rate: 1
  end
  sleep 8
end

blocks.html: Now, keep playing and experimenting until your curiosity about how this all actually works kicks in and you start wondering what else you can do with this. You’re now ready to read the rest of the tutorial.
